title: Discrete, indiscrete, finer, and coarser topologies
terms: discrete topology; indiscrete topology; trivial topology; finer topology; coarser topology.

exposition.text:
The discrete topology is the power set P(X); the indiscrete topology is {∅, X}. A topology T
f
is finer than T when T ⊆ T . Finer means more open sets and therefore more conditions for
c c f
convergence.
The identity from the finer topology to the coarser one is continuous. The reverse identity need
not be. Every function from a discrete space is continuous, and every function into an indis-
crete space is continuous. A discrete space is compact exactly when it is finite; every indiscrete
space is compact.

question.text:
An infinite set X has the discrete topology and the same set Y has the indiscrete topology.
Which statement about the identity bijection f : X → Y is correct?
(A) It is continuous and open.
(B) It is continuous but not open.
(C) It is open but not continuous.
(D) It is neither continuous nor open.
(E) It is a homeomorphism.

solution.text:
Only the preimages of ∅ and Y need to be checked, so f is continuous. A singleton is open
in X but its image is not open in the infinite indiscrete space Y .

question.text:
A set of four points has the indiscrete topology. How many functions from this space to R with
its usual topology are continuous?
(A) 0
(B) 1
(C) 4
(D) Exactly one for each real number.
(E) Every function from the set to R.

solution.text:
If two points have different images, an open interval containing one image and excluding
the other has a nonempty proper preimage, which is not open. Thus exactly the constant
functions are continuous, one for each real value.

question.text:
Let X = {a, b} with a ̸= b, and let x alternate between a and b. What are its sets of limits in
n
the discrete and indiscrete topologies, respectively?
(A) (∅, X) (B) (X, ∅) (C) ({a}, {b}) (D) (∅, ∅) (E) (X, X)

solution.text:
In a discrete space, convergence to a point requires eventual membership in its singleton,
hence an eventually constant sequence. Alternation fails this. In an indiscrete space, the
only open neighborhood of any point is X, which contains every term, so both points are
limits. Finer topologies impose stronger convergence requirements.

question.text:
An infinite set X is given once with the discrete topology and once with the indiscrete topology.
Which statement about compact subsets, with their relative topologies, is correct?
(A) Only finite subsets are compact in either topology.
(B) Every subset is compact in either topology.
(C) Only finite subsets are compact in the discrete topology; every subset is compact in the
indiscrete topology.
(D) Every subset is compact in the discrete topology; only finite subsets are compact in the
indiscrete topology.
(E) No nonempty subset is compact in the indiscrete topology.

solution.text:
A discrete subspace is covered by its singletons, so an infinite one has no finite subcover;
finite spaces are always compact. Every subspace of an indiscrete space is indiscrete, and
any nonempty open cover must contain the whole subspace, giving a one-set subcover. The
empty subspace is compact as well.
